general_information.Description: This course aims to introduce students to behavioral theories of finance and financial decision making. Behavioral foundations including biases; heuristics; and framing effects, will be examined. It then can compare and contrast rational and behavioral theories of finance and financial decision making. This extends students’ knowledge of finance by demonstrating how “real” investors and markets do not always correspond to the rational agents and outcomes described in standard finance courses.
general_information.StudentTasks: - Students must attend at least 80% of contact slots in order to be accepted to the final examination. - Student is responsible to do all exercises, assignments and labs given by instructor in class or at home and submit on time - Use laptop in class only for learning purpose - Promptly access to http://flm.fpt.edu.vn for up-to-date course information

learning_outcomes.CLO Details: Critically review the foundations of conventional finance;
Have a good understand of the main principles of cognitive psychology as applied in behavioural finance;
Understand the causes and nature of market anomalies;
Critically evaluate behavioural influences involving individuals’ securities pricing, financial analysis, investment decisions.
Critically evaluate behavioural influences involving corporate (executive) financial decisions.
Apply the knowledge of behavioural finance to improve investment and corporate performance.
Develop strategies to manage wealth effectively and wisely in inefficient financial markets such as mispriced assets, shocks, news.
Shows self-reliance when working independently and collaboratively
Demonstrate ethical awareness and reflection in business context

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: When eating out, Rory prefers ice-cream over a yogurt. Last night, she had a choice of chocolate ice-cream or milk tea and orange juice and decided on the chocolate ice-cream again. The night before, Rory had a choice of ice-cream, milk tea, or a yogurt, and this time she had milk tea. Then, today, she chose milk tea over a yogurt. Does her selection today indicate that Rory’s choices are consistent with economic rationality? Why or why not?

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: You are considering whether to invest in two stocks, Stock A and Stock B. Stock A has a beta of 1.05 and the standard deviation of its returns has been estimated to be 0.24. For Stock B, the beta is 0.74 and standard deviation is 0.38. a. Which stock is riskier? b. If the risk-free rate is 4% and the market risk premium is 8%, what is the expected return for a portfolio that is composed of 70% A and 30% B? c. If the correlation between the returns of A and B is 0.50, what is the standard deviation for the portfolio that includes 70% A and 30% B?

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: Why might some prefer a combo (fixed price) dinner costing about the same as an à la carte one (where you pay individually for each item)? (Assume the food is identical.)

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: In Finance, the relationship between risk and return is analyzed in the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). From the analysis of survey data it is found that, contrary to the CAPM, executives are likely to expect higher returns from less risky stocks.

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: Refer back to the set of exchange rates in the “Support 3: There are no limits to arbitrage” section in the chapter 3. Describe a profitable arbitrage strategy if x = 110.

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: One potential driver of overconfidence is the self-attribution bias. Define this driver, and provide a concise and clear example of retail investor behavior that was discussed in one of the course papers that may [partly] be explained by biased self-attribution.

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: Prospect Theory was developed by Kahneman and Tversky [1979] as an descriptive alternative to expected utility theory. Briefly discuss the most important differences between the prospect theory approach and the expected utility approach.

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: Why is the disposition effect considered suboptimal behavior?

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: Warren Buffet said, during a shareholder meeting of Berkshire Hathaway, 2006): “It’s like most trends: At the beginning, it’s driven by fundamentals, then speculation takes over. As the old saying goes, what the wise man does in the beginning, fools do in the end. First the fundamentals attract speculation, then the speculation becomes dominant.” c. (6 points) Explain how you recognize the system of fundamentalists, chartists, and switching in this quote.

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: Is this statement true or false? “The disposition effect refers to the preference of investors to sell stocks that have increased in value since bought relative to stocks that have decreased in value since bought.

constructive_questions.Name: HN1
constructive_questions.Details: Mehra and Prescott find that a plausible equity risk premium consistent with a standard general equilibrium model is far lower than the historically observed risk premium over the past hundred years. This is the so-called equity premium puzzle. In standard neo-classical models, the risk premium is often set equal to the product of the coefficient of relative risk aversion and the covariance between stock returns and consumption growth. a. Explain why this relation between consumption growth and stock market returns makes sense.

constructive_questions.Name: HN2
